title: Old Books Likely Being Destroyed to Train AI
paragraphs: Training artificial intelligence requires enormous amounts of text, and books are considered one of the most valuable sources. However, recently unsealed court documents have revealed that the AI company Anthropic bought millions of printed books, scanned them and then destroyed them in order to train its AI model, Claude.

According to documents made public in July 2026 and first reported by The Washington Post, the project, codenamed "Project Panama," began in early 2024. An internal planning document described a plan "to destructively scan all the books in the world." The company also wanted the project to remain secret. Executives reportedly believed that books, especially those published before the internet, would help Claude learn to write well, and that they were free of AI-generated content.

Anthropic bought tens of thousands of books at a time from sellers of used books, such as Better World Books and the UK-based World of Books. It also looked for a company that could scan between 500,000 and two million books over six months. In the scanning process, a hydraulic machine cut off the spines of the books, and the pages were then scanned using industrial equipment. The remaining paper was sent for recycling.

The practice has been considered in court. In a case brought by authors, a US judge ruled in 2025 that using legally purchased books in this way was protected as "fair use" under US law. However, the court treated millions of pirated books that the company had downloaded from the internet differently. Anthropic later agreed to pay $1.5 billion to settle the case, covering about 500,000 works. According to the authors' lead lawyer, it was the largest known copyright recovery in history. An Anthropic lawyer said that the settlement concerned how the materials were acquired, not whether they could be used to develop AI.

The revelations have caused concern. Some commentators believe they show a lack of respect for human creative work. In addition, reports in July 2026 suggested that AI companies might be buying and destroying rare books. However, there is no clear evidence for this, and the court documents suggest that the books were bought in bulk from major sellers.
Other AI companies, including Meta, OpenAI, Google and Microsoft, also face lawsuits from authors.
